Text | Er Mu

Editing | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

Last time, in The world’s strangest-sounding places: Britain, we toured some of Blighty’s fun and peculiar-sounding spots. Now we cross the cold North Sea and head east to Viking territory: Oslo, Norway.

Mention Oslo and many people immediately think of the Impressionist painter Edvard Munch’s famous painting The Scream, or perhaps the film Oslo, about how the Israeli–Palestinian peace accords came to be signed amid the powder keg of the Middle East. The two places we visit this time are barely known at all, but acoustically they are guaranteed to surprise.

A magical ticket hall

It may not transport you to another world like Platform 9¾ at London’s King’s Cross, but the ticket hall at Oslo’s Nationaltheatret station has surprises of its own. Below is a photo of the hall’s interior, with the ticket windows straight ahead. At first glance it looks unremarkable, just an ordinary piece of architecture. So where is the magic? If you keep talking as you walk toward the center of the hall, you’ll notice your voice warbling more and more: a natural tremolo filter!

Listen carefully to the recording below and you’ll hear the effect just described. Toward the end, as the speaker walks away from the center, the warble suddenly and magically disappears.

Multiple echoes are caused mainly by a series of reflections arriving at equal time intervals. When the intervals are slightly unequal, the result is a warbling effect. There is one precondition, of course: the intervals must be long enough, at least 20 ms, for our brain to tell successive echoes apart and hear the sound wavering. The figure below shows the impulse response of the ticket hall, measured with a bursting balloon, followed by the recording itself so you can hear it for yourself.

The figure below is a plan view of the ticket hall. As you can see, the interior is not a simple cylinder but a combination of two cylindrical spaces with different radii. That means sound reflected from the walls of the smaller cylinder returns sooner than sound reflected from the larger one, which may be one reason the reflections arrive at unequal intervals. The real explanation is surely far more complicated; one likely guess is that reflections from the ceiling also strengthen the warble.

There’s a little story that has to be told here: the effect was reportedly never intended. When the ticket hall was first built, the railway company was not at all pleased with the warble inside. But as more and more music lovers came to visit it as a tourist attraction, the company seems to have grown fond of the place, and it set the words “Akustik Skulptur,” Norwegian for “acoustic sculpture,” into the floor.

The Emanuel Vigeland Mausoleum

Four kilometers north of Nationaltheatret station stands another sight that few tourists ever reach: the Emanuel Vigeland Museum. It was originally built by the artist Emanuel Vigeland as a gallery for his work. After his death it was turned into his mausoleum and museum, and the windows of the original room were bricked up. Today every surface in the room is stone or concrete, so sound bounces back and forth inside for a very long time. A Norwegian acoustician and composer has called it the most reverberant space of its size he has ever encountered. Burst a balloon inside, and the bang takes 10 to 15 seconds to die away.

Here is the recording:

The reverberation time is so long that the sound seems to drift slowly down from above, and it is exactly this reverberation that draws so many musicians here.

The video below shows a musician improvising in the space:

Enjoy the music!

(The music combined with the room creates an incredibly dark, medieval atmosphere. You half expect a vampire to leap out at any moment!)

The room is even darker than it looks in the photos above, but once your eyes adjust you’ll make out the huge murals covering the walls and ceiling, on the themes of life, love and death (you can see them in the second half of the video). The entrance is very low, and the artist’s urn sits in a niche right above it, so everyone who enters is forced to bow to him. Rumor has it that this was a kind of posthumous “revenge”: all his life, the artist lived in the shadow of his more successful older brother, the famous Norwegian sculptor Gustav Vigeland.

Artists do love a joke.
